title: Optimal input-sparsity subspace embeddings
formal: Is the optimal-dimension sparse oblivious subspace-embedding conjecture true? Precisely, does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that for every pair of integers \(n\ge d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\), there are an integer \(m\) and a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) over real \(m\times n\) matrices with \[1\le m\le\left\lceil C\,\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil,\qquad s=\left\lceil C\,\frac{\log(d/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\] such that every matrix in the support has at most \(s\) nonzero entries per column and, for every \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pr_{\Pi\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\ \forall x\in W:\ (1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|\Pi x\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\ \bigr]\ge1-\delta?\] The row and column-sparsity bounds must hold simultaneously, with no additional growing factors.
why: Subspace embeddings compress a matrix’s column space while preserving the lengths of all its linear combinations. Small output dimension reduces later computation, and sparse embedding columns reduce the arithmetic needed to apply the map to sparse data. The conjecture asks whether these two advantages can be attained together at the stated dependence on accuracy and failure probability.
status_note: The checked ICALP 2025 and SODA 2026 sources retain the exact dimension/sparsity conjecture. The SODA improvement has sub-polylogarithmic losses and stated parameter restrictions, so it does not settle the all-parameter target here. Bounded later-work searches through 2026-09-15 found no exact resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-status certification.

category_assignment.reason: The target jointly optimizes subspace-embedding dimension and application time, a dimension-reduction question.

importance.reason: This is the precise optimal dimension-versus-sparsity conjecture for oblivious subspace embeddings, a central primitive in fast numerical linear algebra. Resolving the remaining growing factors while preserving failure-probability dependence would identify the attainable compression and application-cost frontier for an extensive class of matrix algorithms.

sentences: An oblivious subspace embedding chooses a random linear map without knowing the subspace it must preserve.
With high probability, the map must preserve the norms of all vectors in each fixed target subspace at once.
The question asks for optimal output dimension together with a precise logarithmic-over-accuracy bound on nonzeros per column.
These two parameters control compression quality and the arithmetic cost of applying the embedding to sparse data.
The checked 2026 result approaches the target with remaining sub-polylogarithmic factors and does not settle the exact conjecture.

definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s survey, in the discussion after Theorem 10, records the proposed row bound \(O((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)\) and input-sparsity application cost involving \(\log(d/\delta)/\varepsilon\). The original title-level card omitted the concrete parameters.

Conjecture 2 of the 2025 ICALP paper states the underlying distributional question explicitly in terms of row dimension and nonzeros per column. This supplies the precise formulation used here, without imposing a particular embedding construction.

The 2025 result reaches optimal row dimension with sparsity \(\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)\) in its stated parameter regime, where that notation hides growing polylogarithmic factors. It therefore does not give the exact logarithmic sparsity bound required here.

The SODA 2026 paper improves the remaining losses to sub-polylogarithmic factors in \(d\) for inverse-polynomially bounded \(\varepsilon\), with a polynomially small failure probability in its headline theorem. Its more detailed Theorem 2.1 gives explicit dimension/sparsity tradeoffs. Neither statement removes all extra factors in the full parameter range of this card.

The preserved norm guarantee concerns one entire fixed subspace. An embedding for selected vectors alone or one constructed using the particular matrix is a different object from an oblivious subspace embedding.
